thread.title: Is Facebook Ready To Break Out?

author: Martin Sosnoff
title: Is Facebook Ready To Break Out?
text:
All macros signal buy growth, the biggest and best. It’s the numero uno market cap, but I’ve x’d out Apple from my buys. Let Warren Buffett hold AAPL for the next 25 years. Too stodgy. Primary category, cell phones, maturing and hard to model. No blockbusters coming out of R&D, as yet. With low inflation and reasonable interest rates, growth stocks do shine. My horses are Alibaba, Facebook, Alphabet, Amazon and Nvidia. Facebook and Alibaba still most misunderstood and underestimated by the Street.
After correcting 15% from its high, FB is poised to move into new high ground. I bought more stock every 10 points down. Maybe I’ll buy some every 10 points up. Facebook comparisons with Apple show higher operating margins at FB, 46% vs. Apple’s 41%. Research spend at Facebook is 18% of revenues, 3 times Apple’s R&D ratio. Year-over-year head count at Facebook rose 48%, an enormous bulge that was accommodated by a surging advertising rate structure.
You could say all this is reflected in disparate price-earnings ratios with FB at 24 times projected 2018 numbers versus Apple a third lower. If the market can like Amazon for its enormous latent earnings power, why can’t you like FB more because the numbers here are jitterbugging?
You learn about building positions by trading in commodities markets. It works just as well on the Big Board. If I could prove Facebook’s advertising rate structure holds firm, I’d pawn my wife’s pearls, earrings and buy more stock. You do what you gotta do to get rich.
Suddenly, rest of the world construes the U.S. as a relatively benign situation even with a disruptive president stirring the pot, daily. How else explain our relatively strong dollar? Boiled down, short the euro and gold and go long the dollar and the S&P 500 Index. Our interest rates on Treasuries ranging from 2-year maturities to 30-year paper is so far above England’s, Germany’s and Japan’s that steady money flow from abroad seems a given for us. Maybe for years unless you see inflation here spiking to 4%.
If inflation comes from wages, materials and oil, I’m dead wrong, and the forward price-earnings ratio of the S&P 500 Index is pared back from 17 times to under 15, even lower if earnings top out. Not my call, but you can model a sizable correction of 10% to 15%. Wall Street lives by what it believes is ahead for the next 12 months. Integral calculus equations do get concocted by assistant professors of finance to prove an efficient stock market exists.
Warren Buffett, in one of his 50-page tours d’horizon in Berkshire Hathaway’s annual report in the early nineties, disposed of the “efficient market” in one sentence, referring to Black Monday, when the market dropped 22%, overnight, near imploding, obviously inefficient. Academics have written dozens of papers rationalizing this event, but they’re baloney.
Black Monday stands, but actually the market topped out August 26, 1987 and fell steadily for weeks. Macros were bad: Interest rates rising, over 7%, weak dollar and a bulging trade deficit. Congress thought insider trading was the gut issue of the decade. The Japanese minister of trade wagged his finger at us and said we were soft, undisciplined and uncompetitive.
Gimme a break! He pontificated just as Japan’s bubble was to reach maximum circumference. Three decades later Nippon has still not gotten over crazy reinvestment in capital goods and real estate while burying its unreported bank rot.
Aside from Black Monday, the Internet bubble of 2000, and the 2008 – ‘09 financial meltdown, we have been investing in a new Gilded Age. But, we’re second derivative. What’s a second derivative? Well, when your hometown sprayed the trees with DDT to kill the mosquitoes, the DDT killed all the town’s cats and then you were overrun with rats. The cats were the second derivative of the DDT. If you can’t link DDT with cats and rats, don’t play in the game.
